title: Adaptive slab reservations and lane fencing: concept
content:
Status: DRAFT - exploring a lightweight reservation primitive ("slab") + lane fencing that balances predictable tenant performance and opportunistic capacity.

Summary
We propose a new capacity primitive called a "slab" (named to emphasize a carved-out chunk of runtime capacity) plus a lightweight "lane fencing" policy that gives tenants a predictable baseline while enabling efficient oversubscription and fast burst behavior without complex cross-tenant credit banking. The approach targets Dedicated customers who need predictable latency for steady traffic but also want low-friction burst behavior during peaks.

Problems we are solving (user/customer pain)
- Customers commit to Dedicated pools but see periodic micro-peaks that cause tail latency spikes or hard throttles.
- Existing reserved vs opportunistic model requires complicated credit scheduling and frequent manual tuning.
- Overprovisioning to avoid spikes is expensive; strict tenant hard-isolation wastes spare headroom.
- Current autoscaler reacts at pool-level and can be slow for short, high-frequency bursts.

Goals
- Provide a predictable per-tenant baseline for latency-sensitive workloads.
- Let low-priority requests opportunistically consume spare capacity without jeopardizing baselines.
- Keep operator and product complexity low (no global ledger service initially).
- Integrate with existing autoscaler: slabs inform scale decisions but do not require tight coupling.
- Support simple admin controls: slab size, reclaim policy, preemption mode, and burst multiplier.

Non-goals
- This is NOT a full replacement for existing burst-credit systems; it is a simpler alternative for many customers.
- Not addressing cross-region spillovers in this initial concept.

High-level design
1) Slab primitive
   - Each tenant can be assigned one or more slabs inside a Dedicated pool. A slab is defined by: size (virtualized concurrency), minimum SLO lane (latency percentile target), reclaim policy (soft | hard), and grace window (seconds).
   - Internally slabs map to token buckets that gate admission into low-latency execution lanes (hot workers/KV-cache priming).

2) Lane fencing
   - Workers in a pool are labeled as "fenced" to one or more slabs or as "opportunistic". Fenced lanes prioritize slab tokens for request routing. Opportunistic lanes accept work if pool utilization < spill_threshold.
   - Fencing enforcement is soft by default: if a slab's tokens are exhausted, requests either queue briefly (preferred) or are routed to opportunistic lanes depending on policy.

3) Burst multiplier and debt
   - Tenants can be allowed a short-duration burst multiplier (e.g., 3x slab for 30s) that creates temporary debt tracked per-slab. Debt decays over a configurable cooldown. Debt influences future slab refill rates.

4) Autoscaler interaction
   - Autoscaler input includes slab saturation metrics: percent of time slabs were token-starved, average queue wait for slab-routed requests, and debt trend.
   - Autoscaler can pre-warm nodes when aggregate slab saturation exceeds a threshold for a sustained window (e.g., 30s).

5) Failover and graceful degradation
   - When pool capacity is constrained, opportunistic lanes are first to be shed, then slabs with soft reclaim. Hard reclaim slabs are immediately evicted to meet higher priority SLOs.
   - A fallback policy can route slab requests to hosted-model endpoints for extremely latency-tolerant workloads.

Example tenant configs (UI/API)
- slab_size: 200 concurrent-token units
- min_slo: p99 < 150ms
- reclaim_policy: soft
- grace_window_sec: 20
- burst_multiplier: 2.5

Operational metrics to emit (early list)
- slab_tokens_total (gauge)
- slab_tokens_used (gauge)
- slab_starve_time_sec (counter)
- slab_queue_latency_p50/p95/p99
- slab_debt_level (gauge)
- opportunistic_lane_utilization (gauge)
- pool_prewarm_trigger_reason (enum tag)

UI and API UX notes
- Console: per-tenant Slabs tab showing configured slab size, debt, and recent starve incidents with timeline view. Quick toggle to change reclaim policy and burst multiplier.
- API: PATCH /v1/dedicated/tenants/{id}/slabs with fields: slab_size, reclaim_policy, grace_window_sec, burst_multiplier.

Rollout plan (phased)
1) Internal alpha (2–4 weeks) - single pool, 3 tenants, manual slab assignment; metrics + debug endpoints; operator-run experiments.
2) Beta (6–8 weeks) - UI controls, automated slab assignment heuristics (suggestion engine based on 95th percentile sustained QPS), autoscaler hooks (read-only) enabled. Invite 5–10 customers.
3) GA (quarterly cadence) - hardened reclaim paths, billing + quota integration, docs, SDK/CLI.

Simulations and cost model notes
- Run synthetic workloads: steady baseline + short spikes (10s–60s) at 2x–5x. Measure p99 tail for slab-routed vs non-slab. Estimate required pool headroom reduction vs current conservative configs.
- Expected win: 20–40% fewer nodes needed to meet latency SLOs for mixed steady+spiky profiles.

Runbook snippets (ops)
- If slab_starve_time_sec > 30s for >5% tenants: trigger emergency prewarm; notify SRE on-call; temporarily increase slab sizes for impacted tenants with soft reclaim.
- If slab_debt_level steadily climbs: evaluate whether burst_multiplier is misconfigured; send recommended adjustments to tenant via account team.

Compatibility and migration
- Default: tenants without slabs remain on current allocation model.
- Migration path: suggest slab_size = 1.2x observed p95 concurrency over last 7 days. Provide console one-click migration.

Open questions / trade-offs
- Token unit semantics: concurrency vs weighted cost (GPU flops / token throughput). Start with concurrency-equivalent tokens for simplicity, phase to model-cost tokens later.
- Debt fairness: how to prevent persistent noisy neighbors from exploiting repeated burst allowances. Options: debt caps, progressive penalties, or temporal backoff.
- Billing model: should slab baseline be billed as committed capacity (fixed) or as a mix (base commit + reserved discount)? Needs finance input.

Next steps (this doc's immediate asks)
- Engineering: quick spike to implement token buckets + routing flags (2 engineers, 2 weeks). Create prototype PR (see linked GH).
- Product: build console mockups and customer-facing FAQ (Sophie).
- SRE: run small internal stress tests and capture metrics to feed autoscaler tuning (Marco).
- Customer outreach: identify 3 pilot customers with bursty-but-latency-sensitive patterns. Reach out via AE (David).

Notes from initial sync
- Marco: prefer queueing + short waiting over immediate spill to opportunistic lanes to preserve cache locality.
- Sophie: UX must make it obvious when a tenant is in "debt" and expected recovery duration.
- David: customers will ask for an SLA on slab baseline once GA; need legal + finance runway.

Links / references
- Prior design that inspired: capacity-sentinel and soft-reserve notes (internal folder) - links above.
- Similar patterns in other infra: Kubernetes vertical-pod-autoscaler and Linux cgroups burst tokens.

Appendix: quick glossary
- slab: a per-tenant reserved execution slot pool with governance parameters.
- fence/lane: worker labeling to prefer (fenced) or accept opportunistic traffic.

-- end of draft --

(Informal notes: this is intentionally lightweight compared to our credit-ledger concepts — aim is to reduce operator mental overhead and make Dedicated a better out-of-box experience for median customers while preserving a migration path to richer models.)
